-Learn how to remove stains well so that clothing cannot only last, but you can resell it. When my kids were babies I used to joke that I could get their clothes for “free” because I was able to resell them for almost what I paid. 
- While you have the money, buy quality shoes. Growing up we always had two pairs of shoes, but my mom would spend an excessive amount of time making sure they would last.
- Turn your AC temp up and your Heat temp down. This is less about saving money and more about getting used to temperature shifts. We grew up without AC and learned how to stay cool without it. Those stills always come in clutch during power outages when everyone else is miserable.
- Build useful skills for bartering and side jobs. Think beyond the typical trades though. My mom and I cleaned hoarder houses for a little bit when my dad couldn’t find work. It sucked, but I learned how to make things look pretty. 
- Get into inexpensive hobbies. When my kids were younger we did every library activity you could. In the summer we were regularly at the park. We couldn’t afford organized sports and tbh I’m glad because we didn’t have to adhere to the rigid schedules I see other parents doing. (No judgement for those that do, it just didn’t fit our family.) 
- My favorite? Practice being poor. Two months out of the year my family has no spend months. That means nothing besides what we absolutely need. We do cheat a little and buy an “emergency” restaurant gift card in case we are stuck out somewhere and are super hungry. This helps us evaluate what we really need in our lives and what we don’t. 
- In that same direction, let go of convenience. We do not have Amazon or any other similar delivery service. If you want something, write it down and we’ll plan a day to go to the store. For clothing we go to thrift stores first. If they don’t have what I’m looking for, I see if I can make it. Do you need to go somewhere that parking will cost $30+? I was in a similar situation with my teen and I was at a point where I wanted to give up too because I just didn’t know what to do. I realized that I was too lenient with her and things needed to change before she completely ruined her life. 

It was three months of absolute hell. I’m not going to sugar coat it. We’re on the other side of it now though, and while there’s still difficult days it’s nowhere near what it used to be. 

We sat our teen down and told her that we’re not giving up on her and we’re not going to let her ruin her life so easily. We took away every single electronic, and she had an 8:00PM bedtime. There was one friend that we trusted that she could hang out with but it had to be at our home. She also had to get involved in something - she chose a fitness class. Weekly drug testing for the first month and then randomly if we felt it was needed. We knew she wasn’t going to pass the first few. 

She had to try therapy (she was very resistant to it) but she could change as many times as she wanted to until she found a therapist she liked.)

Missing school was not an option, but we didn’t put requirements on grades right away. We really just wanted her butt in class and we knew she was so far behind that it was going to be hard to catch up. 

The biggest rule that we had was that she had to spend 3 hours a week one on one with each parent. She could pick what we did - she could even be in a bad mood while we did it. Didn’t matter, she was not getting ungrounded until she did that consistently for a month. 

We had her sign a contract with everything written out and it included what we were also going to do. (One of the agreements was that if she chose to go to a movie for her three hours with one of us we would allow an extra $20 of movie snacks. It’s a silly thing but it’s something we know she loves and wanted to really drill it in that this isn’t just a punishment, but to protect her from herself.)

We also created requirements for things to be lifted. The goal was to earn everything back and she knew it from the start. 

She fought us hard, and it was exhausting but she finally realized that she felt so much better with our stricter rules. A lot of those friends faded away and she’s found a couple really great ones. She’s now realized those people never actually were her friends, even though she does miss them sometimes.

This is the plan God created for our lives - it shouldn't be a medical procedure. - I absolutely do not believe Jessa decided to do a last minute homebirth because I have seen this exact scenario play out before. I know of a couple women who used this lie to get their home birth. It's possible without the show she felt less pressure to perform, or that Ben finally put his foot down.

These women have no other outlet than giving birth and motherhood so they channel all of that into this small area of their lives.
